newsitem.title: USA: NAPM shows manufacturing growing faster in July.
newsitem.headline: NAPM shows manufacturing growing faster in July.

text.p: The U.S. economy continued to grow in July 1997 for the 75th consecutive month, according to a report released Friday by the nation's purchasing managers.
The National Association of Purchasing Managers' Index, which looks at nationwide production, new orders, prices and employment, rose to 58.6 percent in July from 55.7 percent in June.

The PMI report showed economic activity in the manufacturing sector grew at a faster rate in July 1997 than in June, with a dramatic 8.4 percentage point increase in the Production Index to 64.4 percent from 56 percent a month before.

"The overall picture in July as indicated by growth in production, new orders and backlog of orders is one of continued growth in manufacturing activity," Norbert J. Ore, chair of the NAPM Business Survey Committee, said.
"The rate of growth of new orders and production is strong while prices were up for a number of commodities, with 10 industries reporting that they are paying higher prices."
Stocks declined sharply following the release of the report. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 78 points to around 8,145 in mid-morning trading.
"The manufacturing sector grew at a faster pace in July than in June with production and new orders growing at faster rates," Ore said.

NAPM's new orders index rose 2.6 percentage points to 64.6 percent in July, while the backlog of orders reflected a greater volume of unfilled orders during July with the index adding 3 percentage points to 56.5 percent.

"Purchasing executives' comments on business conditions remain optimistic with expectations of continued strength in many businesses. At the same time, a smaller number commented that business is soft. A few expressed concerns about demand exceeding capacity," Ore said in a statement.

Of the 20 industries in the manufacturing sector, 14 reported improvement in July -- miscellaneous (including jewelry, toys, sporting goods, musical instruments); food; paper; stone, clay and aggregate; instruments and photographic equipment; chemicals; petroleum; furniture; industrial and commercial equipment and computers; textiles; fabricated metals; electronic components and equipment; transportation and equipment; and printing and publishing.
Commodities with reports of being in short supply included bearings, ethylene, isopropyl alcohol and galvanised steel, the report said.
Commodities reported with price increases include alcohol, aluminum, caustic soda, chlorine, copper, corrugated containers, ethylene, isopropyl alcohol, praxylene, wastepaper and zinc.
Commodities with price decreases include aluminum, caustic soda, copper, gasoline, natural gas, natural rubber, nicket and steel.
